{{Short description|Probability distribution}}
{{primary sources|date=April 2013}}
In [[probability]] and [[statistics]], the '''generalized beta distribution'''<ref name = McDonald1995>McDonald, James B. & Xu, Yexiao J. (1995) "A generalization of the beta distribution with applications," ''Journal of Econometrics'', 66(1–2), 133–152 {{doi|10.1016/0304-4076(94)01612-4}}</ref> is a [[continuous probability distribution]] with four [[shape parameter]]s, including more than thirty named distributions as [[Limiting case (mathematics)|limiting]] or [[special case]]s. A fifth parameter for [[scale parameter|scaling]] is sometimes included, while a sixth parameter for [[location parameter|location]] is customarily left implicit and excluded from the characterization. The distribution has been used in the modeling of [[income distribution]], stock returns, as well as in [[regression analysis]]. The '''exponential generalized beta (EGB) distribution''' follows directly from the GB and generalizes other common distributions.

== Definition ==
A generalized beta random variable, ''Y'', is defined by the following probability density function (pdf):
:<math> GB(y;a,b,c,p,q) = \frac{|a|y^{ap-1}(1-(1-c)(y/b)^{a})^{q-1}}{b^{ap}B(p,q)(1+c(y/b)^{a})^{p+q}} \quad \quad \text{  for } 0<y^{a}< \frac{b^a}{1-c} , </math>
and zero otherwise. Here the parameters satisfy <math>a \ne 0</math>, <math>0 \le c \le 1</math> and <math>b</math>, <math>p</math>, and <math>q</math> positive. The function ''B''(''p,q'') is the [[beta function]]. The parameter <math>b</math> is the [[scale parameter]] and can thus be set to <math>1</math> [[without loss of generality]], but it is usually made explicit as in the function above. The [[location parameter]] (not included in the formula above) is usually left implicit and set to <math>0</math>.

[[File:GBtree.jpg|thumb|GB distribution tree]]

== Properties ==

=== Moments ===
It can be shown that the ''h''th moment can be expressed as follows:
:<math> \operatorname{E}_{GB}(Y^{h})=\frac{b^{h}B(p+h/a,q)}{B(p,q)}{}_{2}F_{1} \begin{bmatrix}
 p + h/a,h/a;c \\
 p + q +h/a;
\end{bmatrix},
</math>
where <math>{}_{2}F_{1}</math> denotes the [[hypergeometric series]] (which converges for all ''h'' if ''c'' < 1, or for all ''h'' / ''a'' < ''q'' if ''c'' = 1 ).

== Related distributions ==
The generalized beta encompasses many distributions as limiting or special cases. These are depicted in the GB distribution tree shown above. Listed below are its three direct descendants, or sub-families.

=== Generalized beta of first kind (GB1) ===
The generalized beta of the first kind is defined by the following pdf:
:<math> GB1(y;a,b,p,q) = \frac{|a|y^{ap-1}(1-(y/b)^{a})^{q-1}}{b^{ap}B(p,q)} </math>
for <math> 0< y^{a}<b^{a} </math> where <math> b </math>, <math> p </math>, and <math> q </math> are positive. It is easily verified that
:<math> GB1(y;a,b,p,q) = GB(y;a,b,c=0,p,q). </math>
The moments of the GB1 are given by
:<math> \operatorname{E}_{GB1}(Y^{h}) = \frac{b^{h}B(p+h/a,q)}{B(p,q)}. </math>
The GB1 includes the [[Beta distribution|beta of the first kind]] (B1), [[Generalized gamma distribution|generalized gamma]] (GG), and [[Pareto distribution|Pareto]] (PA) as special cases:
:<math> B1(y;b,p,q) = GB1(y;a=1,b,p,q) ,</math>
:<math> GG(y;a,\beta,p) = \lim_{q \to \infty}
GB1(y;a,b=q^{1/a}\beta,p,q) ,</math>
:<math> PA(y;b,p) = GB1(y;a=-1,b,p,q=1) . </math>

=== Generalized beta of the second kind (GB2) ===
The GB2 is defined by the following pdf:
:<math> GB2(y;a,b,p,q) = \frac{|a|y^{ap-1}}{b^{ap}B(p,q)(1+(y/b)^a)^{p+q}} </math>
for <math> 0< y < \infty </math> and zero otherwise. One can verify that
:<math> GB2(y;a,b,p,q) = GB(y;a,b,c=1,p,q). </math>
The moments of the GB2 are given by
:<math> \operatorname{E}_{GB2}(Y^h) = \frac{b^h B(p+h/a,q-h/a)}{B(p,q)}. </math>

The GB2 is also known as the [[Generalized beta prime distribution#Generalization|Generalized Beta Prime]] (Patil, Boswell, Ratnaparkhi (1984)),<ref name = PatilBoswellRatnaparkhi1984>Patil, G.P., Boswell, M.T., and Ratnaparkhi, M.V., Dictionary and Classified Bibliography of Statistical Distributions in Scientific Work Series, editor G.P. Patil, Internal Co-operative Publishing House, Burtonsville, Maryland, 1984.</ref> the transformed beta (Venter, 1983),<ref name = Venter1983>Venter, G., Transformed beta and gamma distributions and aggregate losses, Proceedings of the Casualty Actuarial Society, 1983.</ref> the generalized F (Kalfleisch and Prentice, 1980),<ref name = KalbfleischPrentice1984>Kalbfleisch, J.D. and R.L. Prentice, The Statistical Analysis of Failure Time Data, New York: J. Wiley, 1980</ref> and is a special case (μ≡0) of the [[Pareto distribution#Feller–Pareto distribution|Feller-Pareto]] (Arnold, 1983)<ref name = Arnold1984>Arnold, B.C., Pareto Distributions, Volume 5 in Statistical Distributions in Scientific Work Series, International Co-operative Publishing House, Burtonsville, Md. 1983.</ref> distribution. The GB2 nests common distributions such as the [[generalized gamma distribution|generalized gamma]] (GG), Burr type 3, [[Burr distribution|Burr type 12]], [[Dagum distribution|Dagum]], [[lognormal]], [[Weibull distribution|Weibull]], [[Gamma distribution|gamma]], [[Lomax distribution|Lomax]], [[F-distribution|F statistic]], Fisk or [[Rayleigh distribution|Rayleigh]], [[Chi-squared distribution|chi-square]], [[Half-normal distribution|half-normal]], [[Folded-t and half-t distributions|half-Student's t]], [[Exponential distribution|exponential]], asymmetric log-Laplace, [[log-Laplace distribution|log-Laplace]], [[Power function distribution|power function]], and the [[Log-logistic distribution|log-logistic]].<ref name = McDonald1984>McDonald, J.B. (1984) "Some generalized functions for the size distributions of income", ''Econometrica'' 52, 647–663.</ref>

=== Beta ===
The beta family of distributions (B) is defined by:<ref name=McDonald1995/>
:<math> B(y;b,c,p,q) = \frac{y^{p-1}(1-(1-c)(y/b))^{q-1}}{b^{p}B(p,q)(1+c(y/b))^{p+q}} </math>
for <math> 0<y<b/(1-c) </math> and zero otherwise. Its relation to the GB is seen below:
:<math> B(y;b,c,p,q) = GB(y;a=1,b,c,p,q). </math>
The beta family includes the beta of the first and second kind<ref>Stuart, A. and Ord, J.K. (1987): Kendall's Advanced Theory of Statistics, New York: Oxford University Press.</ref> (B1 and B2, where the B2 is also referred to as the [[Beta prime distribution|Beta prime]]), which correspond to ''c'' = 0 and ''c'' = 1, respectively. Setting <math>c = 0</math>, <math>b = 1</math> yields the standard two-parameter [[beta distribution]].

=== Generalized Gamma ===
The [[generalized gamma distribution]] (GG) is a limiting case of the GB2. Its PDF is defined by:<ref>Stacy, E.W. (1962). "A Generalization of the Gamma Distribution." ''Annals of Mathematical Statistics'' 33(3): 1187-1192. {{JSTOR|2237889}}</ref>
:<math> GG(y;a,\beta,p) = \lim_{q \rightarrow \infty} GB2(y,a,b=q^{1/a} \beta,p,q) = \frac{|a|y^{ap-1}e^{-(y/\beta)^{a}}}{\beta^{ap} \Gamma (p)} </math>
with the <math>h</math>th moments given by
:<math> \operatorname{E}(Y_{GG}^h) = \frac{\beta^h \Gamma (p + h/a)}{\Gamma (p)}. </math>

As noted earlier, the GB distribution family tree visually depicts the special and limiting cases (see McDonald and Xu (1995) ).

=== Pareto ===
The [[Pareto distribution]] (PA) is the following limiting case of the generalized gamma:
:<math>
PA(y;\beta,\theta) = \lim_{a \rightarrow -\infty} GG(y;a,\beta,p=-\theta /a) = \lim_{a \rightarrow -\infty}\left(\frac{\theta y^{-\theta-1}e^{-(y/\beta)^{a}}}{\beta^{-\theta}(-\theta / a)\Gamma(-\theta / a)}\right) = 
</math>
:<math>
\lim_{a \rightarrow -\infty}\left(\frac{\theta y^{-\theta - 1}e^{-(y/\beta)^{a}}}{\beta^{-\theta}\Gamma(1-\theta / a)} \right) = \frac{\theta y^{-\theta - 1}}{\beta^{-\theta}}</math> for <math>\beta < y</math> and <math>0</math> otherwise.

=== Power function ===
The [[power function distribution]] (P) is the following limiting case of the generalized gamma:
:<math>
P(y;\beta,\theta) = \lim_{a\rightarrow\infty}GG(y;a=\theta /p, \beta, p) = \lim_{a\rightarrow\infty}\frac{\mid\frac{\theta}{p}|y^{\theta-1}e^{-(y/\beta)^a}}{\beta^{\theta}\Gamma(p)} = \lim_{a\rightarrow\infty}\frac{\theta y^{\theta - 1}}{p\Gamma(p)\beta^{\theta}}e^{-(y/\beta)^{a}} = 
</math>
:<math>
\lim_{a\rightarrow\infty}\frac{\theta y^{\theta - 1}}{\Gamma(p + 1)\beta^{\theta}}e^{-(y/\beta)^{a}}
= \lim_{a\rightarrow\infty}\frac{\theta y^{\theta - 1}}{\Gamma(\frac{\theta}{a} + 1)\beta^{\theta}}e^{-(y/\beta)^{a}}
= \frac{\theta y^{\theta - 1}}{\beta^{\theta}}</math> for <math>0 < y < \beta</math> and <math>\theta > 0</math>.

=== Asymmetric Log-Laplace ===
The asymmetric log-Laplace distribution (also referred to as the double Pareto distribution <ref>Reed, W.J. (2001). "The Pareto, Zipf, and other power laws." ''Economics Letters'' 74: 15-19. {{doi|10.1016/S0165-1765(01)00524-9}}</ref>) is defined by:<ref>Higbee, J.D., Jensen, J.E., and McDonald, J.B. (2019). "The asymmetric log-Laplace distribution as a limiting case of the generalized beta distribution."''Statistics and Probability Letters'' 151: 73-78. {{doi|10.1016/j.spl.2019.03.018}}</ref>
:<math> 
ALL(y;b,\lambda_1,\lambda_2) = \lim_{a \rightarrow \infty} GB2(y;a,b,p = \lambda_1/a,q = \lambda_2/a) = \frac{\lambda_1\lambda_2}{y(\lambda_1+\lambda_2)}\begin{cases}
  (\frac{y}{b})^{\lambda_1}  & \mbox{for } 0 < y < b \\
  (\frac{b}{y})^{\lambda_2}  & \mbox{for } y \ge b 
\end{cases}
</math>
where the <math>h</math>th moments are given by
:<math> \operatorname{E}(Y_{ALL}^h) = \frac{b^h \lambda_1 \lambda_2}{(\lambda_1 + h)(\lambda_2 - h)}. </math>

When <math>\lambda_1 = \lambda_2</math>, this is equivalent to the [[log-Laplace distribution]].

== Exponential generalized beta distribution ==
Letting <math>Y \sim GB(y;a,b,c,p,q)</math> (without location parameter), the random variable <math>Z = \ln(Y)</math>, with re-parametrization <math>\delta = \ln(b)</math> and <math>\sigma = 1/a</math>, is distributed as an exponential generalized beta (EGB), with the following pdf:
:<math> EGB(z;\delta,\sigma,c,p,q) = \frac{e^{p(z-\delta)/\sigma}(1-(1-c)e^{(z-\delta)/\sigma})^{q-1}}{|\sigma|B(p,q)(1+ce^{(z-\delta)/\sigma})^{p+q}}</math>
for <math> -\infty < \frac{z-\delta}{\sigma}<\ln(\frac{1}{1-c}) </math>, and zero otherwise.
The EGB includes generalizations of the [[Gompertz distribution|Gompertz]], [[Gumbel distribution|Gumbel]], [[Type I extreme value distribution|extreme value type I]], [[Logistic distribution|logistic]], Burr-2, [[Exponential distribution|exponential]], and [[Normal distribution|normal]] distributions. The parameter <math>\delta = \ln(b)</math> is the [[location parameter]] of the EGB (while <math>b</math> is the [[scale parameter]] of the GB), and <math>\sigma = 1/a</math> is the [[scale parameter]] of the EGB (while <math>a</math> is a [[shape parameter]] of the GB); The EGB has thus three [[shape parameter]]s.

Included is a figure showing the relationship between the EGB and its special and limiting cases.<ref>McDonald, James B. & Kerman, Sean C. (2013) "Skewness-Kurtosis Bounds for EGB1, EGB2, and Special Cases," ''Forthcoming''</ref>
[[File:Egbtree.jpg|thumb|The EGB family of distributions]]

=== Moment generating function ===
Using similar notation as above, the [[moment-generating function]] of the EGB can be expressed as follows:
:<math> M_{EGB}(Z)=\frac{e^{\delta t}B(p+t\sigma,q)}{B(p,q)}{}_{2}F_{1} \begin{bmatrix}
 p + t\sigma,t\sigma;c \\
 p + q +t\sigma;
\end{bmatrix}.
</math>

== Multivariate generalized beta distribution ==

A multivariate generalized beta pdf extends the univariate distributions listed above.  For <math>n</math> variables <math>y = (y_1 , ... , y_n)</math>, define <math>1xn</math> parameter vectors by <math>a = (a_1 , ... , a_n)</math>, <math>b = (b_1 , ... , b_n)</math>, <math>c = (c_1 , ... , c_n)</math>, and <math>p = (p_1 , ... , p_n)</math> where each <math>b_i</math> and <math>p_i</math> is positive, and <math>0</math> <math>\le</math> <math>c_i</math> <math>\le</math> <math>1</math>.  The parameter <math>q</math> is assumed to be positive, and define the function <math>B(p_1, ... , p_n, q)</math> = <math>\frac{\Gamma(p_1)...\Gamma(p_n)\Gamma(q)}{\Gamma(\bar{p}+q)}</math> for <math>\bar{p}</math> = <math>\sum_{i=1}^{n} p_i</math>.

The pdf of the multivariate generalized beta (<math>MGB</math>) may be written as follows:

:<math>MGB(y; a, b, p, q, c) = \frac{(\prod_{i=1}^{n} |a_i|y_i^{a_i p_i - 1})(1 - \sum_{i=1}^{n} (1-c_i)(\frac{y_i}{b_i})^{a_i})^{q - 1}}{(\prod_{i=1}^{n} b_i^{a_i p_i})B(p_1, ... , p_n, q)(1 + \sum_{i=1}^{n} c_i(\frac{y_i}{b_i})^{a_i})^{\bar{p} + q}}</math>

where <math>0</math> <math><</math> <math>\sum_{i=1}^{n} (1-c_i)(\frac{y_i}{b_i})^{a_i}</math> <math><</math> <math>1</math> for <math>0</math> <math>\le</math> <math>c_i</math> <math><</math> <math>1</math> and <math>0</math> <math><</math> <math>y_i</math> when <math>c_i</math> = <math>1</math>.

Like the univariate generalized beta distribution, the multivariate generalized beta includes several distributions in its family as special cases. By imposing certain constraints on the parameter vectors, the following distributions can be easily derived.<ref name = CockrielMcDonald2017>William M. Cockriel & James B. McDonald (2017): Two multivariate generalized beta families, Communications in Statistics - Theory and Methods, {{doi|10.1080/03610926.2017.1400058}}</ref>

=== Multivariate generalized beta of the first kind (MGB1) ===

When each <math>c_i</math> is equal to 0, the MGB function simplifies to the multivariate generalized beta of the first kind (MGB1), which is defined by:

:<math>MGB1(y; a, b, p, q) = \frac{(\prod_{i=1}^{n} |a_i|y_i^{a_i p_i - 1})(1 - \sum_{i=1}^{n} (\frac{y_i}{b_i})^{a_i})^{q - 1}}{(\prod_{i=1}^{n} b_i^{a_i p_i})B(p_1, ... , p_n, q)}</math>

where <math>0</math> <math><</math> <math>\sum_{i=1}^{n} (\frac{y_i}{b_i})^{a_i}</math> <math><</math> <math>1</math>.

=== Multivariate generalized beta of the second kind (MGB2) ===

In the case where each <math>c_i</math> is equal to 1, the MGB simplifies to the multivariate generalized beta of the second kind (MGB2), with the pdf defined below:

:<math>MGB2(y; a, b, p, q) = \frac{(\prod_{i=1}^{n} |a_i|y_i^{a_i p_i - 1})}{(\prod_{i=1}^{n} b_i^{a_i p_i})B(p_1, ... , p_n, q)(1 + \sum_{i=1}^{n} (\frac{y_i}{b_i})^{a_i})^{\bar{p} + q}}</math>

when <math>0</math> <math><</math> <math>y_i</math> for all <math>y_i</math>.

=== Multivariate generalized gamma ===

The multivariate generalized gamma (MGG) pdf can be derived from the MGB pdf by substituting <math>b_i</math> = <math>\beta_i q ^ {\frac{1}{a_i}}</math> and taking the limit as <math>q</math> <math>\to</math> <math>\infty</math>, with Stirling's approximation for the gamma function, yielding the following function:

:<math>MGG(y; a, \beta, p) = (\frac{(\prod_{i=1}^{n} |a_i|y_i^{a_i p_i - 1})}{(\prod_{i=1}^{n} \beta_i^{a_i p_i})\Gamma(p_i)})e^{- \sum_{i=1}^{n} (\frac{y_i}{\beta_i})^{a_i}} = \prod_{i=1}^{n} GG(y_i; a_i, \beta_i, p_i)</math>

which is the product of independently but not necessarily identically distributed generalized gamma random variables.

=== Other multivariate distributions ===

Similar pdfs can be constructed for other variables in the family tree shown above, simply by placing an M in front of each pdf name and finding the appropriate limiting and special cases of the MGB as indicated by the constraints and limits of the univariate distribution.  Additional multivariate pdfs in the literature include the [[Dirichlet distribution]] (standard form) given by <math>MGB1(y; a = 1, b = 1, p, q)</math>, the [[Beta prime distribution|multivariate inverted beta]] and [[Inverted Dirichlet distribution|inverted Dirichlet]] (Dirichlet type 2) distribution given by <math>MGB2(y; a = 1, b = 1, p, q)</math>, and the multivariate Burr distribution given by <math>MGB2(y; a, b, p, q = 1)</math>.

=== Marginal density functions ===

The marginal density functions of the MGB1 and MGB2, respectively, are the generalized beta distributions of the first and second kind, and are given as follows:

:<math>GB1(y_i; a_i, b_i, p_i, \bar{p} - p_i + q) = \frac{|a_i|y_i^{a_i p_i - 1}(1 - (\frac{y_i}{b_i})^{a_i})^{\bar{p} - p_i + q - 1}}{b_i^{a_i p_i}B(p_i, \bar{p} - p_i + q)}</math>

:<math>GB2(y_i; a_i, b_i, p_i, q) = \frac{|a_i|y_i^{a_i p_i - 1}}{b_i^{a_i p_i}B(p_i, q)(1 + (\frac{y_i}{b_i})^{a_i})^{p_i + q}}</math>

== Applications ==
The flexibility provided by the GB family is used in modeling the distribution of:
* distribution of income
* hazard functions
* stock returns
* insurance losses

Applications involving members of the EGB family include:<ref name=McDonald1995/><ref name=McDonald1984/>
* partially adaptive estimation of regression models
* time series models
* (G)ARCH models

=== Distribution of Income ===
The GB2 and several of its special and limiting cases have been widely used as models for the distribution of income. For some early examples see Thurow (1970),<ref name=Thurow1970>Thurow, L.C. (1970) "Analyzing the American Income Distribution," ''Papers and Proceedings, American Economics Association'', 60, 261-269</ref> Dagum (1977),<ref name=Dagum1977>Dagum, C. (1977) "A New Model for Personal Income Distribution: Specification and Estimation," ''Economie Applique'e'', 30, 413-437</ref> Singh and Maddala (1976),<ref>Singh, S.K. and Maddala, G.S (1976) "A Function for the Size Distribution of Incomes," ''Econometrica'', 44, 963-970</ref> and McDonald (1984).<ref name=McDonald1984/>
Maximum likelihood estimations using individual, grouped, or top-coded data are easily performed with these distributions.

Measures of inequality, such as the [[Gini index]] (G), Pietra index (P), and [[Theil index]] (T) can be expressed in terms of the distributional parameters, as given by McDonald and Ransom (2008):<ref name=McDonaldRansom>McDonald, J.B. and Ransom, M. (2008) "The Generalized Beta Distribution as a Model for the Distribution of Income: Estimation of Related Measures of Inequality", ''Modeling the Distributions and Lorenz Curves'', "Economic Studies in Inequality: Social Exclusion and Well-Being", Springer: New York editor Jacques Silber, 5, 147-166</ref>
:<math>\begin{align} G=\left({\frac{1}{2\mu}}\right) \operatorname{E}(|Y-X|) = \left(P{\frac{1}{2\mu}}\right) \int_{0}^{\infty}\int_{0}^{\infty} |x-y|f(x)f(y)\,dx dy \\
= 1 - \frac{\int_{0}^{\infty} (1-F(y))^2\,dy}{\int_{0}^{\infty} (1-F(y))\,dy} \\
P = \left( \frac{1}{2\mu}\right) \operatorname{E} (|Y-\mu|) = \left(\frac{1}{2\mu}\right)\int_0^{\infty} |y-\mu|f(y)\, dy \\
T = \operatorname{E} (\ln (Y/\mu)^{Y/\mu}) = \int_0^ \infty (y/\mu) \ln (y/\mu) f(y)\, dy
\end{align}</math>

=== Hazard Functions ===
The [[hazard function]], h(s), where f(s) is a pdf and F(s) the corresponding cdf, is defined by
:<math> h(s) = \frac{f(s)}{1-F(s)} </math>

Hazard functions are useful in many applications, such as modeling unemployment duration, the failure time of products or life expectancy. Taking a specific example, if s denotes the length of life, then h(s) is the rate of death at age s, given that an individual has lived up to age s. The shape of the hazard function for human mortality data might appear as follows: decreasing mortality in the first few months of life, then a period of relatively constant mortality and finally an increasing probability of death at older ages.

Special cases of the '''generalized beta distribution''' offer more flexibility in modeling the shape of the hazard function, which can call for "∪" or "∩" shapes or strictly increasing (denoted by I}) or decreasing (denoted by D) lines. The '''generalized gamma''' is "∪"-shaped for a>1 and p<1/a, "∩"-shaped for a<1 and p>1/a, I-shaped for a>1 and p>1/a and D-shaped for a<1 and p>1/a.<ref>Glaser, Ronald E. (1980) "Bathtub and Related Failure Rate Characterizations," ''Journal of the American Statistical Association'', 75(371), 667-672 {{doi|10.1080/01621459.1980.10477530}}</ref> This is summarized in the figure below.<ref>McDonald, James B. (1987) "A general methodology for determining distributional forms with applications in reliability," ''Journal of Statistical Planning and Inference'', 16, 365-376 {{doi|10.1016/0378-3758(87)90089-9}}</ref><ref name=McDonaldRichards>McDonald, J.B. and Richards, D.O. (1987) "Hazard Functions and Generalized Beta Distributions", ''IEEE Transactions on Reliability'', 36, 463-466</ref>
